questions.text: A building has 150 m² interior walls and 200 m² exterior walls. Interior: 10 m²/L per coat (2 coats). Exterior: 12 m²/L per coat (2 coats, rough concrete reduces by 15%). Calculate total paint needed with 5% waste.

rationale.a: 47.2 L is too low; may omit one surface or coat.
rationale.b: 55.3 L is intermediate; possibly missing exterior roughness adjustment.
rationale.c: 61.5 L may result from applying waste incorrectly or using wrong coverage.
rationale.correct: Interior: (150 ÷ 10) × 2 = 30 L. Exterior adjusted coverage = 12 × 0.85 = 10.2 m²/L. Exterior: (200 ÷ 10.2) × 2 = 39.2 L. Total base = 30 + 39.2 = 69.2 L. With 5% waste: 69.2 × 1.05 = 72.66 L ≈ 72.8 L.
rationale.takeaway: For mixed surfaces: calculate each type separately (adjusting coverage for condition), sum, then apply waste factor.

questions.text: The formula for paint required is ___.

rationale.a: Multiplying area by coverage rate would give m⁴/L (incorrect units).
rationale.c: Adding area and coverage rate is meaningless mathematically.
rationale.d: Dividing coverage rate by area gives L/m⁴ (inverse and incorrect).
rationale.correct: Paint required (liters) = Total area (m²) ÷ Coverage rate (m²/L). Dividing area by the coverage rate gives liters needed.
rationale.takeaway: Always divide area by coverage rate: Paint (L) = Area ÷ Coverage rate.

questions.text: When paint coverage is reduced due to surface roughness, the factor applied is typically ___.

options.text: Multiply coverage rate by 1.15–1.20 to account for increased surface area and ensure adequate coverage
Divide area by 1.15–1.20, adjusting for the rough texture that increases paint consumption
Add 15–20% to paint volume to compensate for the additional material needed on rough surfaces

rationale.b: Multiplying by >1 would increase coverage, which is incorrect.
rationale.c: Dividing area by a factor is an alternative approach, but the standard method is to adjust the coverage rate downward.
rationale.d: Adding a percentage to paint volume is a result, not the direct adjustment factor.
rationale.correct: Rough surfaces reduce effective coverage. If coverage is 10 m²/L and roughness reduces it by 20%, then effective coverage = 10 × 0.80 = 8 m²/L. This increases paint needed.
rationale.takeaway: To account for rough surfaces, reduce the coverage rate by 15–20% (multiply by 0.80–0.85).

questions.text: How much interior latex paint (at 10 m²/L coverage) is needed for 100 m² of wall with one coat?

rationale.c: 50 liters results from multiplying 100 × coverage rate (inverse formula).
rationale.d: 100 liters is the total area, not paint volume.
rationale.takeaway: Use the formula: Area ÷ Coverage rate = Paint needed.

questions.text: A commercial complex requires 500 m² of interior wall coating (primer + finish) at 10 m²/L coverage per coat, plus 600 m² of exterior wall coating (rough concrete, one coat only, nominal coverage 12 m²/L, reduce by 25% for roughness). Calculate total paint needed with 10% waste and determine the number of 20-liter containers required.

rationale.a: 125 L and 7 containers is too low; may omit a coat or misapply waste.
rationale.b: 167 L and 9 containers is close to base amount but misses waste and rounding.
rationale.d: 220 L and 12 containers over‑estimates paint needed.
rationale.correct: Interior: (500 ÷ 10) × 2 = 100 L. Exterior adjusted coverage = 12 × 0.75 = 9 m²/L. Exterior: 600 ÷ 9 = 66.67 L (one coat). Total base = 100 + 66.67 = 166.67 L. With 10% waste: 166.67 × 1.10 = 183.33 L ≈ 184 L. 20‑liter containers: 184 ÷ 20 = 9.2 → round up to 10 containers.
rationale.takeaway: Multi‑area, multi‑coat systems: calculate each area and coat combination separately, sum, apply waste, then convert to container count rounding up.

questions.text: A rough concrete wall (60 m²) requires painting. The coverage rate is normally 10 m²/L, but rough surfaces reduce coverage by 20%. How much paint is needed for two coats?

rationale.a: 6 L is one coat on smooth surface (60 ÷ 10).
rationale.b: 12 L is two coats on smooth surface without adjusting for roughness.
rationale.d: 18 L may result from applying a waste factor or incorrectly doubling the adjustment.
rationale.correct: Adjusted coverage = 10 m²/L × 0.80 = 8 m²/L. Per coat: 60 ÷ 8 = 7.5 L. Two coats: 7.5 × 2 = 15 L.
rationale.takeaway: Adjust coverage rate for surface condition BEFORE calculating paint volume. Rough surfaces reduce effective coverage by 15–20%.

questions.text: A contractor estimates 40 liters of paint at 550 pesos per liter. How many 4-liter cans are needed, and what is the total cost?

rationale.a: 10 cans at 22,000 pesos assumes no waste, but rounding up for waste is standard practice.
rationale.b: 11 cans at 22,000 pesos incorrectly uses 40 L for cost while rounding cans up.
rationale.correct: Base estimate is 40 L, but a 10% waste allowance (common in painting) brings total to 44 L. 44 L ÷ 4 L/can = 11 cans. Cost = 44 L × 550 pesos/L = 24,200 pesos.
rationale.takeaway: Always account for waste (typically 5–10%) and round up to full cans. Cost = total liters × price per liter.

questions.text: A project requires 80 m² of wall painting with primer (11 m²/L) and finish coat (10 m²/L). How many total liters are needed?

rationale.a: 14.5 L is too low; may result from using an average coverage without correct division.
rationale.c: 18 L may include a waste factor not stated in the problem.
rationale.d: 28.6 L results from adding 80 ÷ 11 + 80 ÷ 10 incorrectly or using the wrong formula.
rationale.takeaway: For multi-coat systems, calculate each coat's paint volume separately, then sum.

questions.text: A typical coverage rate for interior latex paint is ___.

rationale.a: 5 m²/L is too low; applies only to specialty coatings or epoxy.
rationale.b: 8 m²/L is low-end; applies to rough surfaces or specialty products.
rationale.d: 15 m²/L is high; applies to thin primer or water-based stains, not standard latex.
rationale.correct: Interior latex paint typically covers 10 m²/L on smooth surfaces. This is a standard benchmark.
rationale.takeaway: Standard interior latex paint covers approximately 10 m²/L per coat on smooth surfaces.

questions.text: A standard paint can size in the Philippines is ___.

rationale.a: 0.5 L, 2 L, 5 L are less common sizes.
rationale.c: 2 L, 10 L, 50 L are non-standard in Philippines.
rationale.d: Gallon sizes are sometimes used, but the common local standard is metric: 1 L, 4 L, 20 L.
rationale.correct: Philippine standard paint cans are 1 L (single/small), 4 L (1 gallon equivalent), and 20 L (5 gallons or bulk). These are the market standard sizes.
rationale.takeaway: Philippine paint cans: 1 L, 4 L, 20 L. These are the sizes to convert liter estimates into can quantities.
